People think a board runs a company, and it does not. A board does three things and everything else is noise. It checks the numbers, it argues with the strategy, and it hires or fires the person at the top. That is the whole job. What surprises people who join a board for the first time is how much of it is reading. The material is sent out a week in advance, it is read on a plane, and by the time everybody is in the room the real work has already been done in private. So the meeting itself is not where decisions are made. It is where they are confirmed, or where somebody says the thing that nobody had written down. And that is why I take the informal parts seriously. If a report is submitted and approved and nobody ever asks the analyst who wrote it a single question, the board has learned exactly nothing that was not already on the page.

I have run corporate year-end events for fifteen years, and the thing nobody tells you is that the party is a working meeting with better food. Legally it is treated as an extension of the workplace, which is why we are so careful about how it is organised. But that is not the interesting part. The interesting part is who talks to whom. On a normal working day, an analyst three levels down is never in the same room as somebody from the board, and even if they were, there would be an agenda and no reason to speak. At the party there is no agenda. So the conversations that happen are the ones people actually want to have, and I have watched careers turn on ten minutes next to a table. My advice is always the same and people always ignore it. Do not spend the evening with the colleagues you see every day. You already know what they think.
